note: ph.u_len is attacker-controlled from the packed file header. When ph.u_len < 64 (sizeof(Elf64_Ehdr)), the expression umin64(MAX_ELF_HDR_64, ph.u_len) - sizeof(Elf64_Ehdr) underflows to a huge unsigned value, so the division yields a large number and the check passes even for a large u_phnum.

The decompressed data is written into the MemBuffer u of size ph.u_len. The decompressed ELF header contains e_phnum (u_phnum) set to a large value (e.g., 0xFFFF), which is read from the decompressed bytes.

code: phdr = (Elf64_Phdr *) (void *) (1+ ehdr); for (unsigned j=0; j < u_phnum; ++phdr, ++j)
note: The loop iterates u_phnum times, but the MemBuffer u only has ph.u_len bytes (less than 64). The first phdr read at offset 64 already reads past the end of the buffer, and subsequent iterations read further out of bounds.
get_te32 reads 4 bytes from phdr->p_type which is at offset 64+0 from the start of the buffer. Since ph.u_len < 64, this read is out of bounds.
get_te64 reads 8 bytes from phdr->p_filesz which is at offset 64+32 from the start of the buffer. This 8-byte read is completely past the end of the MemBuffer u, causing the heap-buffer-overflow.
Entry point of the vulnerable function. The attacker-controlled packed file triggers the OOB read when the unpack routine processes the malformed ELF header with insufficient bounds validation.
